tip: For an action happening right now, use stare plus the gerund: sta lavorando (is working), not just lavora.
Italian makes yes/no questions by intonation alone. Sei fidanzata? keeps the same word order as the statement.
The accented è, as in Lui è dentro, means is; the plain e with no accent means and.
Adjectives ending in -e like veloce keep one form for both genders; a woman is also veloce.
Adjectives ending in -e switch to -i in the plural: disponibile becomes disponibili for a group.
Adjectives match the speaker's gender: a man says curioso, a woman says curiosa.
The subject pronoun is dropped here; the -i ending of sei already tells you it means you.
In the past tense, già (already) sits between hai and the participle: hai già mangiato.
Ci here means each other: ci sentiamo is we hear from one another, a common way to say talk soon.
Use uno instead of un before s plus a consonant: uno sconto, uno studente.
Masculine words starting with a vowel take lo, shortened to l': l'ospedale.
Italian often uses the present for near-future plans: fai domani literally is do tomorrow.
Impersonal si means one or you-in-general: si pronuncia asks how it is pronounced.
Le is the polite to you here: quanto le devo asks how much I owe you formally.
After vuoi, the second verb stays in the infinitive: vuoi uscire, not vuoi esci.
A past participle used as an adjective agrees in gender: colazione is feminine, so compresa ends in -a.
Some set phrases drop the article: a scuola means at school, with no la needed.
In orario is a fixed phrase meaning on time; keep in with no article.
Singular family members skip the article with possessives: mia moglie, not la mia moglie.
Feminine una shortens to un' before a vowel: un'amica. Masculine un takes no apostrophe.
Dito is irregular: one is il dito, but several become le dita, switching to feminine plural.
Da means from: da qui is from here, so lontano da qui asks the distance from here.
Dire has the irregular past participle detto: hai detto means you said, never hai dicuto.
An object pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive: indicare plus mi becomes indicarmi.
Before another pronoun, mi changes to me: me lo puoi spiegare is can you explain it to me.
After a preposition, tu becomes te: orgoglioso di te, never di tu.
Negatives come in pairs: non plus mai means never, and both words are kept: non sta fermo mai.
To ask whose, Italian uses di chi, literally of whom: di chi è questo libro.
Su plus il merges into one word, sul: sul letto means on the bed.
Weather uses fare, not essere: fa caldo means it's hot, and fa freddo means it's cold.
Nascere, to be born, forms its past with essere: è nato means he was born.
Countries take in with no article: in Italia, in Francia. È nata in Italia is born in Italy.
Cities take a, not in: va a Milano means goes to Milan.
Amica adds an h in the plural to keep the hard c sound: amica becomes amiche.
Nouns ending in -ista are the same for men and women; only the article shows gender: l'elettricista.
